newsitem.title: FRANCE: Car bomb kills 12 south of Algiers - state radio.
newsitem.headline: Car bomb kills 12 south of Algiers - state radio.

text.p: A car bomb killed 12 people and wounded 31 in Boufarik, a town south of the capital Algiers, on Thursday, a state-run Algerian radio station said.

A Western diplomat based in Algiers told Reuters the bombing aimed to disrupt preparations for June 5 parliamentary elections, the North African country's first since Moslem guerrillas took up arms to topple the government five years ago.
The car bomb exploded shortly before noon in the centre of Boufarik, killing 12 people and wounding 31, state-run Chaine III radio said, quoting security forces.
"A huge explosion took place...in the city centre where election campaign and meetings were expected to take place," a Boufarik resident said.
Armed security forces surrounded the area, stopped traffic in a radius of nearly one km (half a mile) and prevented people from getting near the explosion site, he added.
Boufarik, 25 km (16 miles) south of Algiers, is in the heart of a rich farming area and is close to the Moslem fundamentalist stronghold of Blida province.
"It undoubtedly aims to create artificial tension to disrupt the polls of June 5," the Western diplomat said.

Boufarik is in the centre of an strategic area which both the authorities and the guerrillas are struggling to control and "is well protected by self-defence units and armed local militias against Moslem rebels", the diplomat added.
Algerian officials were not available for comment.

The official Algerian news agency APS said civilian protection units and security forces arrived immediately to give help to Boufarik's victims of what it called "this criminal act". It put the toll at nine killed and 33 wounded.
Neither APS nor the radio commented on who might be behind the bombing.
Earlier this month a car bomb killed four people and wounded 21, many of them schoolchildren, in Algiers.

Moslem guerrillas launched their armed campaign against the government in 1992 after authorities cancelled general elections which the Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) was poised to win. About 60,000 people have been killed in the political violence.
This week the government offered residents up to 4.5 million dinars ($80,000) for information leading to the capture or killing of Algeria's most wanted guerrillas.
The proposed reward appeared in posters put up on walls in several suburbs of Algiers, residents speaking by telephone from the Algerian capital said on Tuesday.

Topping the list of names on the posters were Antar Zouabri, leader of the Armed Islamic Group (GIA), Madani Mezrag of the rival Islamic Salvation Army (AIS), the armed wing of the outlawed FIS, and his deputy Ahmed Benaicha, they said.
The government also offered up to three million dinars ($53,000) for tipoffs on three leading guerrilla figures -- Said Makhloufi, Mustapaha Kartali and Miloud Habbi.
